title: Assessing Fitness to Travel: Practical Cases in Air Travel and Chronic Disease Management
description: Case-based quiz (Q1–Q10) covering COPD and hypoxia testing, post-MI/PCI air travel, and the multi-morbid traveller. Source: lecture slides, 2026-10-16.

questions.text: Case 1 — COPD: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV₁ 38% predicted), not on home O₂, breathless after two flights of stairs, last exacerbation 8 weeks ago, resting SpO₂ 93%, plans a 9-hour flight. What is the most appropriate next step in assessing his fitness to fly?
options: Fit to fly without further assessment, because resting SpO₂ is >90%
Prescribe in-flight oxygen immediately, because FEV₁ is <40% predicted
Detailed pre-flight assessment (resting SpO₂, functional capacity) and consider formal hypoxia testing
Repeat spirometry now and base the decision primarily on the current FEV₁

questions.text: Case 1 — COPD (cont.): Which feature in this patient most strongly supports proceeding to formal hypoxia testing before a long-haul flight?
options: Age of 68 years alone
Former smoking history
FEV₁ 38% predicted with resting SpO₂ 93% on room air
Not currently using home oxygen

questions.text: Case 1 — COPD (cont.): His hypoxic challenge test gives PaO₂ 7.0 kPa (53 mmHg) with SpO₂ 82%, and he remains clinically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: No special arrangement is needed, because PaO₂ remains >50 mmHg
Recommend in-flight supplemental oxygen and arrange the airline's oxygen requirements in advance
Cancel all air travel permanently, because the HCT is abnormal
Start long-term home oxygen before the trip as soon as possible

questions.text: Cardiovascular disease: A 55-year-old had an uncomplicated STEMI treated with successful primary PCI, preserved EF and no arrhythmia. He wants the earliest reasonable date to take a 2-hour flight. What do you advise?
options: He should never fly again
From about 3 days (many clinicians advise 7–10 days)
Only after 3 months
Only after a normal exercise stress test, which is mandatory

questions.text: Case 2 — Recent NSTEMI: A 60-year-old woman had an NSTEMI 5 days ago (drug-eluting stent to the LAD, EF 45%, no arrhythmia or heart failure, on DAPT) and is booked on a 13-hour flight on day 9. What is the most important consideration in deciding whether she can fly?
options: The fact that she is receiving dual antiplatelet therapy
Whether the MI and PCI have been clinically uncomplicated and she is stable
Whether her EF has returned to ≥55%
Whether she has been discharged from hospital for at least 7 days

questions.text: Case 2 — Recent NSTEMI (cont.): What additional concern is particularly relevant because this is a 13-hour long-haul flight?
options: Increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and the challenges of prolonged immobility
Increased risk of acute stent thrombosis caused directly by cabin pressure
A predictable reduction in EF caused by the lower cabin oxygen concentration
Loss of antiplatelet effect caused by prolonged exposure to cabin altitude

questions.text: Case 2 — Recent NSTEMI (cont.): Before completing the airline's MEDIF, which finding would most strongly support advising her to postpone the flight?
options: Clinically stable, no chest pain or heart failure, and walks without significant symptoms
She is taking DAPT following implantation of a drug-eluting stent
Persistent/recurrent chest pain, decompensated heart failure, or another sign of ongoing cardiac instability
EF 45% with no symptoms or clinical evidence of heart failure

questions.text: Case 3 — Multi-morbid traveller: A 72-year-old woman (insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, stable HF NYHA II, DVT 3 years ago) had an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy 6 days ago and plans an 11-hour flight across 7 time zones in 3 days. Which best summarizes the key issues before clearance?
options: Recent surgery and advanced age are the main concerns; diabetes and heart failure are unlikely to matter
Glycemic control is the main concern; her previous DVT is too remote to be clinically relevant
Recent surgery, previous DVT, insulin-treated diabetes, stable heart failure and prolonged travel all matter
Surgery was uncomplicated and heart failure is stable, so no additional assessment is necessary

questions.text: Case 3 — Multi-morbid traveller (cont.): She will be 9 days post-laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the day of departure. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: Any flight within 2 weeks of abdominal surgery is contraindicated
Timing may be acceptable after uncomplicated laparoscopic surgery if she has recovered well, without complications
Postpone until at least 6 weeks after surgery because of the risk of wound dehiscence
The flight is safe solely because laparoscopic surgery does not affect fitness to fly

questions.text: Case 3 — Multi-morbid traveller (cont.): Before completing the airline's medical form, which is the most appropriate plan for this patient?
options: Usual insulin unchanged, oral hydration, and compression stockings only, as her DVT was 3 years ago
Time-zone-adjusted insulin/glucose plan, individualised VTE-prophylaxis assessment, confirm recovery and airline plans
Hold insulin on the travel day; use aspirin for VTE prophylaxis, as anticoagulation is unnecessary
Delay until a full 6-week recovery regardless of clinical status; restart usual medications on arrival
